chapterTitle: The Seventy Sent, the Samaritan's Mercy, and the Good Part
themeTitle: The One Thing That Cannot Be Taken Away

scripture.text: Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place, where he was about to come.
scripture.understanding: The travel narrative widens beyond the Twelve as Jesus commissions a larger circle — seventy (many manuscripts read seventy-two), a number that echoes the seventy nations of Genesis 10 and the seventy elders of Moses in Numbers 11. They go 'two by two' and 'ahead of him': every laborer is an advance party preparing towns for the King's own arrival.

scripture.text: Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out laborers into his harvest.
scripture.understanding: Before strategy comes prayer. The bottleneck is never a shortage of harvest — the fields are already white — but a shortage of harvesters. Notice the holy irony: you pray to the Lord of the harvest, and then you become the very answer you prayed for, sent out into the field yourself.

scripture.text: Go your ways. Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves.
scripture.understanding: Jesus tells no comfortable lie. He does not send them out as an army but as lambs — defenseless, exposed — into a pack of wolves. The mission's safety is never in their own teeth and claws, but in the Shepherd who does the sending.

scripture.text: Carry no purse, nor wallet, nor sandals. Greet no one on the way.
scripture.understanding: Travel light and travel urgent. No purse, no spare bag, no extra sandals — utter dependence on God's provision through the people they serve. 'Greet no one on the way' is not rudeness but urgency; roadside greetings were long ceremonies, and the King's business will not wait.

scripture.text: Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house.’
scripture.understanding: The first gift they carry is peace. In Jesus' mouth 'peace' is not a mere pleasantry but the Hebrew shalom — wholeness, the shelter of the Kingdom — spoken like a tangible blessing meant to settle on a home.

scripture.text: If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; but if not, it will return to you.
scripture.understanding: The spoken blessing is treated almost as a living thing: it lands and rests on a 'son of peace' — one open to receive it — and, if refused, it returns to the speaker undiminished. No blessing you offer in Jesus' name is ever wasted.

scripture.text: Remain in that same house, eating and drinking the things they give, for the laborer is worthy of his wages. Don’t go from house to house.
scripture.understanding: Stay put; do not shop around for better hospitality. The worker deserves support, so receive it without shame — but do not turn the mission into a hunt for the most comfortable table.

scripture.text: Into whatever city you enter, and they receive you, eat the things that are set before you.
scripture.understanding: Eat what is set before you — a quiet loosening of food boundaries that already leans toward the coming Gentile mission. The messenger's freedom and gratitude at the table become part of the witness.

scripture.text: Heal the sick who are therein, and tell them, ‘God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’
scripture.understanding: Healing is the sign; the nearness of the Kingdom is the message. The two go together — the mercy that mends bodies is the visible advertisement that God's reign has walked up to the door.

scripture.text: But into whatever city you enter, and they don’t receive you, go out into its streets and say,
scripture.understanding: Rejection is anticipated and answered with dignity, not retaliation. Where a town closes its doors, the messengers do not curse or brawl — they make a public, prophetic declaration in the streets.

scripture.text: ‘Even the dust from your city that clings to us, we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’
scripture.understanding: Shaking off the dust is a prophetic sign of separation — 'we take nothing of you, not even your dirt.' Yet even over those who reject it, the messengers still preach the same sentence: the Kingdom has come near. Their refusal does not un-say the good news.

scripture.text: I tell you, it will be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city.
scripture.understanding: To reject the Kingdom when it walks up to your door is a graver thing than the notorious sin of Sodom. Light received brings blessing; light deliberately refused brings a heavier accounting.

scripture.text: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.
scripture.understanding: The woe falls on the Galilean towns that saw the most and repented the least. Pagan Tyre and Sidon would have turned to God in sackcloth had they witnessed such miracles — so the privileged towns that saw Jesus and merely shrugged are more culpable than the cities they despised.

scripture.text: But it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the judgment than for you.
scripture.understanding: Judgment is weighed by opportunity. The more revelation you receive, the higher the accounting; wasted light is not neutral — it deepens guilt.

scripture.text: You, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades.
scripture.understanding: Capernaum, Jesus' ministry home base, presumed itself lifted to heaven by its privilege. But privilege without repentance does not raise you — it only sets you higher so the fall is farther, all the way down to Hades.

scripture.text: Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me. Whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me.”
scripture.understanding: The stakes of the mission are made personal and cosmic. To hear the seventy is to hear Jesus; to reject them is to reject Jesus — and to reject Jesus is to reject the Father who sent him. The messenger carries the authority of the One who sends.

scripture.text: The seventy returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!”
scripture.understanding: The seventy come back electric with joy — even the demons submitted. Notice the fine print of their own report: it was 'in your name,' not their own. The authority was borrowed, and it worked.

scripture.text: He said to them, “I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven.
scripture.understanding: Jesus reads the cosmic meaning behind a handful of village exorcisms. The small victories in Galilee are tremors of a war already decided; he watched the ancient enemy crash from his usurped height like a lightning bolt — sudden, total, irreversible.

scripture.text: Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will in any way hurt you.
scripture.understanding: He hands them real, delegated authority — to tread on serpents and scorpions (the venom of the enemy) and over all the enemy's power. The promise is of ultimate protection: nothing will finally, spiritually harm the one on his mission.

scripture.text: Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”
scripture.understanding: The crucial correction. Do not build your joy on spiritual power — power intoxicates and deceives. Build it on the one unshakable fact: your name is written in heaven, enrolled in the Lamb's book. Ministry results fluctuate; your enrollment in heaven does not.

scripture.text: In that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit, and said, “I thank you, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight.”
scripture.understanding: One of the rare glimpses of Jesus openly rejoicing — and Luke tells us it is joy 'in the Holy Spirit.' He thanks the Father that the Kingdom's secrets bypass the clever and the credentialed and land in the laps of 'little children,' the humble who simply receive.

scripture.text: Turning to the disciples, he said, “All things have been delivered to me by my Father. No one knows who the Son is, except the Father, and who the Father is, except the Son, and he to whomever the Son desires to reveal him.”
scripture.understanding: The astonishing claim of exclusive intimacy: everything has been handed to the Son, and the Father and the Son know each other completely and reciprocally. No one reaches the Father by cleverness — only by the Son's choosing to reveal him. Salvation is a gift of revelation, not a prize of intellect.

scripture.text: Turning to the disciples, he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes which see the things that you see,
scripture.understanding: Privately, Jesus pronounces the disciples' eyes blessed. What they are watching is not ordinary — it is the arrival of everything the prophets strained toward.

scripture.text: for I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them, and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them.”
scripture.understanding: Prophets and kings — David, Isaiah, and their kind — ached to see this day and died before it dawned. The disciples are watching, in real time, the fulfillment all of redemptive history leaned toward. Their privilege is staggering — and it demands a response.

scripture.text: Behold, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
scripture.understanding: A lawyer — an expert in the Torah — rises to test Jesus with the ultimate question: how to inherit eternal life. He comes not to learn but to spar, hoping to trap the teacher.

scripture.text: He said to him, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?”
scripture.understanding: The master teacher answers a question with a question, turning the man back to the Scripture he claims to master: not just 'what is written' but 'how do you read it' — how does it actually land in your life?

scripture.text: He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.”
scripture.understanding: The lawyer answers rightly, fusing Deuteronomy 6:5 with Leviticus 19:18 — love God with your whole being, and love your neighbor as yourself. The entire law hangs on these two hooks.

scripture.text: He said to him, “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.”
scripture.understanding: 'You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.' The trap snaps shut on the trapper — he already knows the right answer; his problem was never information. The command is do, not merely know.

scripture.text: But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?”
scripture.understanding: Now the man's real motive surfaces: 'desiring to justify himself.' He hunts for a loophole, a boundary line — 'Who counts as my neighbor?' — hoping to shrink the circle of obligation down to something he has already achieved.

scripture.text: Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
scripture.understanding: Jesus refuses to define 'neighbor' and tells a story instead. A man on the notoriously dangerous Jerusalem-to-Jericho road is ambushed, stripped, beaten, and left half dead — anonymous and unidentifiable, just a bleeding body in a ditch.

scripture.text: By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
scripture.understanding: A priest — a professional of holiness — comes down the same road, sees the man, and deliberately crosses to the far side. His religion had detailed rules about corpse-defilement; it had no reflex of mercy.

scripture.text: In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place, and saw him, passed by on the other side.
scripture.understanding: A Levite, another temple servant, does exactly the same. Two representatives of Israel's religious system see the need and choose their own convenience and ritual purity over the dying man.

scripture.text: But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
scripture.understanding: Then the shock: a Samaritan — the despised half-breed heretic, the last person a Jewish audience would ever cast as hero — comes, sees, and is moved with compassion, gut-wrenched to the core. Jesus makes the enemy the hero to detonate the lawyer's neat categories.

scripture.text: came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
scripture.understanding: Compassion becomes costly, hands-on action. He binds the wounds, pours on his own oil and wine (medicine and antiseptic), puts the man on his own animal while he walks, and personally nurses him at an inn. Real mercy always ends up in the body — sleeves rolled, hands dirty.

scripture.text: On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, and gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
scripture.understanding: The mercy does not stop at first aid. He pays two denarii (two days' wages) up front, opens an unlimited line of credit — 'whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay' — and promises to return. This is mercy that keeps paying long after the crisis is over.

scripture.text: Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
scripture.understanding: Jesus flips the lawyer's question inside out. The man asked, 'Who is my neighbor?' (whom must I love?). Jesus asks, 'Who proved to be a neighbor?' (whom did love make?). Neighbor is not a category to define but a person to become.

scripture.text: He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”
scripture.understanding: The lawyer cannot even say the word 'Samaritan'; he manages only 'He who showed mercy.' And Jesus drives the whole Gospel of Luke into three words: 'Go and do likewise.' The answer to 'what must I do to inherit eternal life' collapses into doing this.

scripture.text: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
scripture.understanding: The scene shifts to a home. Martha takes the initiative of hospitality and welcomes Jesus in — a good and generous act. She is the host, and there is nothing wrong with that.

scripture.text: She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word.
scripture.understanding: Her sister Mary takes the posture of a disciple — sitting at the Teacher's feet, hearing his word. In that culture, to sit at a rabbi's feet was the seat of a student; Mary, a woman, quietly claims the disciple's place, and Jesus lets her keep it.

scripture.text: But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
scripture.understanding: Martha is 'distracted' — literally pulled in many directions by much serving. Her frustration boils over into blaming both her sister and, tellingly, Jesus himself: 'Don't you care?' Good work, soured by anxiety, curdles into accusation of God.

scripture.text: Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
scripture.understanding: Jesus answers with tender repetition — 'Martha, Martha' — and names not her serving but her inner state: anxious and troubled, fretting over many things. He diagnoses the heart, not the to-do list.

scripture.text: but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”
scripture.understanding: Above the many things there is one thing — and Mary has chosen the good part, the good portion, which will not be taken away from her. Sitting at his feet and receiving his word is the one imperishable choice, a treasure no circumstance can confiscate.

visualMeditations.title: Lambs Sent Into the Wolf Pack
visualMeditations.image: Picture a shepherd opening the gate — not to bring the lambs in for the night, but to send them out. Out past the safety of the fold, straight onto a hillside where the wolves are already circling, ears back, teeth bared. No armor, no fangs, no claws. Just wool and soft feet walking deliberately toward the predators.
visualMeditations.meaning: Jesus refuses to lie about the cost. The mission is not to a friendly world; it is exposed, vulnerable, and dangerous. Yet the lamb's security was never its own defenses — it is the authority and provision of the One who does the sending. The Kingdom advances not by out-muscling the world but by the strange power of vulnerable obedience.

visualMeditations.title: Satan Falling Like Lightning
visualMeditations.image: A black night sky, and then a single searing bolt — not drifting gently down, but slamming from the height of heaven to the earth in a fraction of a second, blinding and irreversible. Blink and you missed the descent; all that remains is the scorched afterimage. That is what Jesus says he watched happen to the ancient enemy.
visualMeditations.meaning: While the seventy were rejoicing over a handful of demons obeying in some Galilean village, Jesus was reading the cosmic scoreboard. Those small victories were tremors of an already-decided war. The prince of this world is a defeated foe crashing from his usurped throne — and every act of Kingdom obedience is another flash of that same lightning.

visualMeditations.title: Moved in the Gut on the Jericho Road
visualMeditations.image: The Jerusalem-to-Jericho road: seventeen miles plunging through bleak red rock and blind curves, bandit country the locals called the Bloody Pass. A man lies in the dust, stripped naked so you cannot read his tribe, beaten senseless so you cannot hear his accent, half dead. Two holy men glance, calculate, and drift to the far edge of the road. Then the wrong man kneels down into the blood — and something deep in his gut turns over.
visualMeditations.meaning: The priest and the Levite had a theology; the Samaritan had a stomach that churned. Splanchnizomai is a visceral word — mercy you feel in your body before your mind can tally the cost. Jesus deliberately makes the heretic the hero to shatter the lawyer's tidy categories: the man who looks least like God acts most like him.

visualMeditations.title: At the Feet or in the Kitchen
visualMeditations.image: One house, two sisters. Mary is on the floor at the Teacher's feet, perfectly still, drinking in every word. Martha is a blur of motion in the next room — pots, fire, sweat, the clatter of much serving — shooting glances at her seated sister with rising resentment, until she finally erupts and drags Jesus into the quarrel.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is not lazy versus hardworking; it is anxious versus attentive. Martha's genuinely good work has soured into worry and accusation ('Lord, don't you care?'). Jesus does not scold service — he reorders it. One thing is needed, and it is not another dish; it is the seat Mary took. Presence before performance, or the performance will eat you alive.

structure.label: The Sending of the Seventy (v. 1-12)
structure.body: Jesus commissions seventy laborers, sends them out light and vulnerable to preach peace and the nearness of the Kingdom, and warns of the weight of rejection.

structure.label: Woes on the Unrepentant Cities (v. 13-16)
structure.body: The privileged Galilean towns that saw the most miracles and repented least face a heavier judgment than pagan Tyre, Sidon, and even Sodom.

structure.label: The Return and the Fall of Satan (v. 17-20)
structure.body: The seventy return rejoicing that demons obeyed; Jesus confirms the cosmic victory but redirects their joy from power to their names written in heaven.

structure.label: The Son Rejoices; the Father Revealed (v. 21-24)
structure.body: Jesus rejoices in the Spirit that the Kingdom is revealed to little children, claims exclusive intimacy with the Father, and blesses the disciples' eyes.

structure.label: The Lawyer and the Good Samaritan (v. 25-37)
structure.body: A lawyer's self-justifying question, 'Who is my neighbor?', is answered by the parable in which a despised Samaritan, not the priest or Levite, becomes the picture of neighbor-love: 'Go and do likewise.'

structure.label: Mary and Martha (v. 38-42)
structure.body: In a home, Martha's anxious serving is gently reordered beneath Mary's choice to sit at Jesus' feet — the one good part that will not be taken away.

sections.heading: The Wrong Man as the Hero: Mercy Without Borders
paragraphs: The lawyer's question — 'Who is my neighbor?' — is a request for a boundary. He wants a line that tells him where his obligation to love safely ends, because every definition of 'neighbor' is secretly also a permission slip for whom he is allowed to ignore. Jesus refuses to draw that line. Instead he tells a story in which the two men best qualified to help — a priest and a Levite, career professionals of God — fail, and the one man least qualified in Jewish eyes, a Samaritan (a despised, half-pagan heretic), becomes the living icon of God's own heart.

Then Jesus reverses the grammar of the question itself. The lawyer asked, 'Who qualifies as the object of my love?' Jesus asks, 'Who became a neighbor by loving?' Neighbor is not a status other people hold or fail to hold; it is an identity you take on when compassion moves you across the road. So the command 'Go and do likewise' is not an invitation to admire a moving story — it is an order to enter it. To inherit eternal life is not to define love with precision but to do it with your own two denarii, your own animal, and your own hands.

sections.heading: Rejoice Not in Power, but in a Name Written in Heaven
paragraphs: The seventy came back high on success — even the demons obeyed. Jesus does not deny the power; he had given it (v. 19), and he confirms its cosmic weight by declaring he saw Satan fall. But he plants a warning flag right in the middle of their victory party: do not let your joy rest on what you can do, not even on genuine, God-given spiritual power. Power is real, but it is a treacherous foundation for the soul — it swells the ego, it rises and falls with results, and, chillingly, Jesus says elsewhere that some who cast out demons in his name he will tell, 'I never knew you' (Matthew 7:22-23).

The only stable joy is a name written in heaven — an enrollment in the Book of Life that rests entirely on grace, not on performance. This is the very truth that then bursts out of Jesus himself in verse 21: the Father reveals the Kingdom not to the wise and clever who think they have earned it, but to little children who simply receive it. The whole chapter drives one nail all the way home — your worth is not in your usefulness; it is in being known, chosen, and written down by God.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: Jesus builds his answer on Leviticus 19:18 — 'love your neighbor as yourself' — and the rest of the New Testament seizes that command as the beating heart of the whole law. Paul writes in Galatians 5:14, 'For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' and again in Romans 13:9-10 that 'love is the fulfillment of the law.' James 2:8 calls it 'the royal law.' The Good Samaritan is that royal law walking on two feet — and the early church heard something deeper still: the ultimate Good Samaritan is Jesus himself, who found us stripped and half dead on the road, was moved with compassion, bound up our wounds, paid a debt we could never pay, and promised, 'I will repay you when I return.' We are told to 'go and do likewise' precisely because he did it first for us.

And when Jesus says, 'I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven' (v. 18), he is reading a few village exorcisms as skirmishes in a cosmic war whose ending is already written. Revelation 12:9-10 unfolds the same scene on the grand scale — 'the great dragon was thrown down... the accuser of our brothers... has been thrown down' — and Paul promises the church in Romans 16:20, 'The God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet.' The authority to 'tread on serpents and scorpions' (v. 19) directly echoes the first gospel promise of Genesis 3:15, that the woman's seed would crush the serpent's head. Every demon that bows to Jesus' name is one more flash of that same lightning — yet the believer's final security is not the power to tread on serpents, but the name written safe in heaven (Revelation 21:27).

lexicon.insight: Literally 'to be moved in the splanchna' — the bowels, the guts, which the Greeks regarded as the seat of the deepest emotions. This is not a polite, arm's-length pity but a visceral churn, a physical wrench in the belly. In the Gospels the verb is used almost exclusively of Jesus himself (and of the father in the Prodigal, and the king in the parable of debts). Luke deliberately pours God's own gut-level mercy into the body of a despised Samaritan — the compassion of God shows up wearing the wrong face.

Literally 'the one near.' The lawyer wants it as a noun — a fixed category with an edge he can stand safely outside of. Jesus turns it into a verb of the heart. By the end of the parable 'neighbor' is no longer a question of who qualifies for your love but of who you become when love moves you toward the one bleeding in the ditch. The word shifts from a boundary you draw to a person you become.

Active compassion — not merely a feeling but a deed. It is the Greek word standing behind the Hebrew chesed, God's covenant loving-kindness. The lawyer cannot bring himself to say 'the Samaritan'; he says only 'the one who did eleos.' The whole towering question — 'What must I do to inherit eternal life?' — collapses into this single word made flesh in action. Mercy is love with its sleeves rolled up.

The seventy return with chara over their newfound power (v. 17). Then Jesus reroutes that rejoicing — do not celebrate that spirits obey, but that your names stand written in heaven (v. 20) — and in that same hour he himself leaps for joy in the Holy Spirit (v. 21). Luke's Gospel is soaked in joy from Mary's Magnificat to the angels' Gloria — but here Jesus teaches the anatomy of stable joy. Do not peg your gladness to what you can do, which rises and falls; peg it to whose you are, which never changes. Joy grounded in grace cannot be voted out by a bad day.

A 'share, portion, allotment' — the word used for a slice of an inheritance or a plot of land divided among heirs. Mary has chosen the good meris. This lands with Old Testament thunder: the Levites received no land because 'the Lord is their portion' (Numbers 18:20), and David sings, 'The Lord is my chosen portion... a beautiful inheritance' (Psalm 16:5-6). Mary, at his feet, has chosen the Lord himself as her inheritance — and that title deed, Jesus says, will not be taken away from her.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is pressing one question into you through this whole chapter: what are you actually building your life on — your usefulness, your success, your busyness — or the one thing that can never be taken away?

items.title: The Danger of the Demons Being Subject to You
items.body: The seventy came home glowing because it worked — even the demons obeyed. And Jesus, in the middle of the celebration, gently pulled the rug: 'Don't rejoice in that.' Ministry success is one of the most seductive spiritual traps there is, because it feels holy. Do you measure your standing with God by your results, your gifts, your platform, your numbers? Then what happens to your peace on the days nothing 'works,' when the prayer isn't answered and the door stays shut? Hear the Spirit: your name was written in heaven on your worst day just as surely as on your best. Is your joy anchored there, or is it riding the scoreboard?

items.title: The Neighbor You Are Crossing the Street to Avoid
items.body: The priest and the Levite were not cartoon villains. They were busy, religious, respectable, and self-protective — men with real reasons to keep walking. That is exactly why the parable is dangerous to you. Who is the bleeding person your schedule and your comfort keep stepping around? The relative you have written off, the coworker who is drowning, the poor man you have trained yourself not to see? Is your religion long on rules and short on the gut-level mercy that gets its hands dirty? The Spirit will not let you admire this story from a safe distance. Name the person. Then go and do likewise.

items.title: Martha's Kitchen or Mary's Feet
items.body: The sin in this house is not laziness — it is good service that has quietly curdled into anxious self-importance and accusation of God: 'Lord, don't you care?' Martha was doing something genuinely good for Jesus while resenting the very Jesus she was serving. Where has your doing for God slowly replaced your being with God? Could you sit at his feet with nothing to accomplish and nothing to offer, and simply receive his word — or would you fidget until you found something to fix? The Spirit is asking: are you troubled about many things, when only one is needed?

audit.title: The Scoreboard Check
audit.body: What is your joy actually pegged to this week — your name written in heaven, or your name doing well down here (your wins, your reputation, your productivity)? Be brutally honest: if all your visible results vanished tomorrow, how much of your peace would go with them?

audit.title: The Ditch You Walk Past
audit.body: Name the specific person or need you have been 'passing by on the other side.' What convenient reason have you been leaning on — too busy, too costly, not my problem, not my kind of person — to keep from stopping?

audit.title: Distracted or Devoted
audit.body: Is your service to God flowing out of real time at his feet, or has the serving quietly become a substitute for the sitting? When did you last simply hear his word with no task attached — just Mary's seat, nothing to produce?

practices.title: Do One Costly 'Likewise'
practices.body: This week, pick the one person in your ditch and physically cross the road toward them. Bind a wound with your time, your money (your own 'two denarii'), or your hands — do the mercy, do not merely feel it. Write down now: who, and by when. Then close the loop and actually do it.

practices.title: Take the Mary Seat
practices.body: Tomorrow, before you do a single thing for God, sit for fifteen minutes at his feet with the open Word and no agenda but to hear. Choose the good part before the many things start shouting. Do this first, every morning, for one week, and watch how it reorders everything that follows.

prayerReflection: Lord of the harvest, here I am — send me. I am a lamb among wolves, and my safety is not my own strength but the Shepherd who sends me, so I go carrying nothing but the peace of Your Kingdom. Guard me from the intoxication of my own usefulness; let me not rejoice merely that things obey me, but rejoice that my name is written in heaven — a treasure no failure, no enemy, and no bad day can ever take away. Father, Lord of heaven and earth, You hide these things from the wise and reveal them to little children; make me low enough to receive. Break my heart with the compassion that broke Yours — when I see the one beaten and half dead in the ditch, do not let me pass by on the other side. Teach me to stop asking 'who is my neighbor?' and to simply become one, showing mercy with my hands, my time, and my own two denarii. And in all my serving, keep me from Martha's anxious, distracted, accusing heart. Let me choose the one thing that is needed. Let me choose Mary's good part — the seat at Your feet, hearing Your word — the portion that will never be taken away from me. In Jesus' name, Amen.

storyConnections.title: Moses and the Seventy Elders
storyConnections.summary: When the weight of leading Israel crushed Moses, God told him to gather seventy elders; the Lord took of the Spirit on Moses and put it on the seventy, and they prophesied. Two of them, Eldad and Medad, prophesied back in the camp, and when Joshua tried to stop them, Moses answered, 'Would that all the Lord's people were prophets, that the Lord would put his Spirit on them!' Luke's seventy, sent out in the Spirit's power ahead of Jesus, are the answer to Moses' longing — the mission of God widening far beyond one man, until the whole people carry the word.

storyConnections.title: The Men of Samaria Who Showed Mercy
storyConnections.summary: In one of Scripture's most startling scenes, the army of Samaria took two hundred thousand captives of Judah. But the prophet Oded confronted them, and the leaders of Ephraim clothed the naked, gave them sandals, fed them, anointed their wounds, set the feeble on donkeys, and carried them to Jericho. Centuries later Jesus tells a parable in which a Samaritan clothes, anoints with oil, sets a wounded Judean on his own animal, and provides for him near that same Jericho road. Jesus is very likely reaching back to a real memory of Samaritan mercy to shame a lawyer who thought no good could come from Samaria.

storyConnections.title: Mary Who Kept Choosing His Feet
storyConnections.summary: The Mary who sat listening at Jesus' feet in Luke 10 shows up again in John's Gospel — and both times she is at his feet. When Lazarus died, she fell at his feet weeping, and Jesus wept with her before raising her brother. Then, days before the cross, she broke a jar of costly perfume over Jesus' feet and wiped them with her hair, while others complained about the waste. The woman who chose the 'good part' that would not be taken away spent her life proving it: the seat at his feet became devotion, and the devotion became worship poured out.
